turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come on through. What brings you in?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, g'day doc. Traffic was a shocker, took us ages down the freeway. Anyway, umm, I'm 74 and it's the waterworks, I'm up and down all night for a wee and the stream's gone weak.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Karen, his daughter. I stayed over last week and I counted, Dad, you were up five times.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): No, love, that's not right. It's three, sometimes four. You counted when I got up for a glass of water and stood at the window.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I still reckon it was five, at least one of those nights. I was awake with the dog.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so you two don't quite agree on the number. Ray, you're saying three or four, and the stream is weak. Anything else when you pass urine?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah it dribbles at the end. I stand there like a dill waiting for it to finish. Been like that a fair while.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have the night-time trips and the weak stream been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, I can't pin it. Last winter, or the one before. Maybe around the grand final, maybe after, I honestly don't know.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): And I still have my cuppa in the evening. Two teas after dinner, well actually sometimes it's just one if the cricket's on and I'm dozing. Probably doesn't help the bladder, but I like it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine at all?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never seen any blood. Not once.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): While we're on it, he nicked his shin on the rose bush. That cut healed in five days, no drama.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah that was nothing. Cleaned it, gone in five days. The roses are going mad, I should prune them before they take over the path.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good that it healed up promptly. Separate question, any fevers?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fevers.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Chest is fine, no cough.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that shifted at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't think so. Maybe a bit. The trousers feel looser, but I've been walking the dog more, so it's hard to say really.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He doesn't take his blood pressure tablets on Sundays. I've seen the blister pack still full.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not Sundays. It's Saturdays. Bowls day. I get home and I forget the tablet. Every other day is fine.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me get the medicine straight. Which blood pressure tablet, and what dose?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The perindopral, uh, 5 mg, one in the morning. The chemist knows it. I've been on it for years for the blood pressure.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perindopril 5 mg each morning. And you miss it on Saturdays after bowls, not Sundays. I'll note Saturdays.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep, that's the one. My brother Kevin had his prostate out, oh, six or seven years back. He lives up in Cairns now, mad on the fishing.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. You're up three or four times by your count, Karen heard five, the stream is weak with dribbling, no blood, evening tea, and the timing is vague, last winter or the one before. Blood pressure is ongoing, perindopril 5 mg, missed on Saturdays.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's pretty fair, yeah. Apart from Karen's counting. She means well.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): This pattern fits an enlarged prostate, the benign sort, as a working impression. I can't call it definite today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Righto. Not keen on an operation if I can help it. A mate at bowls had something done and he talked about it for a month.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No operation on the table today. I'd like a PSA blood test and a urine test, both booked from here, to look at the prostate and to check the urine.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): PSA, yeah, I've heard of that one. Do I have to fast? I had a bacon roll on the way, bit late if I do.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No fasting for these. And I'd like to start tamsulosin, a capsule by mouth, 400 micrograms at night, for the stream and the night-time wees.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Tamsolosin? Will that make me dizzy? I don't want to fall over at bowls.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tamsulosin. It can make some blokes light-headed when they stand, especially the first few doses, so stand up slowly, and take it after you've eaten.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I'll give it a go.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Also, ease off the tea in the evening, keep it earlier in the day if you can. And please take the perindopril on Saturdays too, even after bowls. An alarm on your phone helps.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, fair enough. The tea will be the hard bit. I can do an alarm, I think. Karen bought me one of those phones and I only use it to ring her.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll remind him Saturday arvo when I ring, if he hasn't already taken it.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in four weeks with the results, and we'll see how the tamsulosin is sitting. If you suddenly can't pass urine at all, that's straight to the hospital, don't wait.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Got it. I'll drag Karen along if she's not on shift. Thanks, doc.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No worries. Reception will have the forms on your way out.

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: A caregiver or relative reports observations ('the cut healed in five days', 'she sleeps badly', 'he does not take the tablets on Sundays'); the patient agrees, disagrees or corrects one point. The nurse also reports a measurement that the patient mentioned before.
traps.label_rule: reported_by follows who said it. A healing cut that healed normally is a negative finding (no slow-healing wounds) or nothing, NOT a symptom. A disputed fact is recorded with certainty disputed or as an uncertainty. A correction replaces the earlier value (Saturday, not Sunday).

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Breathing trouble was asked, but patient only said chest is fine, no cough.
bad.text: Shortness of breath (status=absent, assertion=negative, reported_by=patient, temporality=current)

omissions.text: Recorded as weight loss present, but the patient only said weight change was uncertain: 'I don't think so. Maybe a bit. The trousers feel looser... hard to say really.'
The patient specifically denied ever seeing blood in the urine: 'No. Never seen any blood. Not once.'
Family history detail missing: brother Kevin had his prostate out 6 or 7 years ago.
No fasting was required for the planned PSA blood test and urine test.
